summary: For ages 7–9, learners locate the Amazon on a map of South America, name at least two of the nine countries it spans, and connect its record-breaking statistics (world's largest river by water volume; roughly 10% of all known species; ~40,000 plants, ~1,300 birds, ~3,000 fish) to concrete comparisons they can picture. The teaching sequence starts from the map (giving the numbers 'a place to live') before attaching awe-anchoring superlatives. Core misconceptions to confront: the Amazon as a single country/only-Brazil, 'largest river' meaning longest rather than greatest water volume, and '10% of species' meaning 10 species rather than one tenth of all kinds of life. These figures are estimates, not fixed exact counts.
misconceptions: 'The Amazon is one country / in Brazil only' — it spans nine countries.
'The Amazon is the LONGEST river' — the claim taught here is largest by WATER VOLUME/discharge (Nile length is debated separately).
'10% of species means 10 species' — it means one tenth of ALL kinds of living things on Earth.
'A rainforest and its river are the same thing' — the forest is the habitat; the river runs through it.
'These numbers are exact and fixed' — they are estimates; many species remain undiscovered.

activities.title: Find it on the map, then name the countries
steps: Locate the shaded Amazon basin on a map of South America.
Name at least two countries the Amazon spreads across (e.g. Brazil, Peru, Colombia).
State in your own words that the Amazon is a rainforest spanning nine South American countries — not a single country and not only Brazil.
activities.insight: The Amazon is Earth's greatest rainforest that crosses nine countries; it is a habitat, not a nation, and the river runs through the forest rather than being the same thing as it.

activities.title: Largest by water, not by length
steps: Consider the question 'Which river carries the most water on Earth?' and predict before the answer is shown.
Compare a thick bar representing the Amazon's water volume against bars for other major rivers (e.g. Nile, Mississippi) and describe what 'largest' means here.
State clearly that the Amazon is the largest river by water volume (discharge), and explain why this is different from being the longest.
activities.insight: 'Largest river' in this topic means greatest water volume/discharge — the Amazon moves more water than the next several giant rivers combined — which is a distinct claim from how long a river is.

activities.title: What '10% of all species' really means
steps: Look at a row of ten Earth pictures that together stand for all the known kinds of life on Earth, with each picture standing for one tenth. Shade one picture to show the roughly 10% of all those species that live in the Amazon.
Explain in your own words that this means roughly 1 in every 10 kinds of living thing on Earth lives here — not 10 species.
Read the record cards (about 40,000 plant species, 1,300 bird species, 3,000 types of fish) and name at least two specific biodiversity numbers.
Say why biodiversity means huge VARIETY of different kinds, not just 'lots of animals'.
activities.insight: Biodiversity is about the variety of distinct kinds of life; the Amazon holds about one tenth of all known species on Earth, an extraordinary concentration of different living things.

activities.title: Explain why the Amazon is special (diagnostic discussion)
steps: Respond to the prompt: 'Someone says the Amazon is a country in Brazil. Is that right? Tell me what the Amazon actually is, and then why it's such a special place for wildlife.'
Give a corrected description: Earth's greatest rainforest across nine South American countries, with the largest river by water volume.
Explain WHY so much life lives there — linking the richness to the hot, wet climate rather than only restating numbers.
activities.insight: A learner who understands this topic can correct the country/length/scale errors and give a reason for the Amazon's biodiversity, not just recite facts.

checkQuestion: Someone says 'the Amazon is a country in Brazil.' Is that right? Tell me what the Amazon actually is, and then tell me WHY it's such a special place for wildlife.
checkAnswer: No — the Amazon isn't a country. It's Earth's greatest rainforest, spreading across nine countries in South America (not just Brazil), and it holds the world's largest river by water volume. It's special for wildlife because it's home to about 10% of all the species on Earth — tens of thousands of plants, over a thousand kinds of bird, thousands of fish — more variety of life than almost anywhere else.
